subject: geography
title: Rivers & Coasts Adventure: Management
welcome_lead: Holderness is losing 2 metres of cliff a year. Should we build a wall — or move back?
meta_desc: GCSE Geography coastal and river management — hard and soft engineering, case studies.
final_note: You compared hard vs soft engineering and explored Holderness coast case study.

concepts.def: Wood/rock fence into sea — traps sand
Adding sand to widen a beach naturally
Letting low-value land flood — relocating people

walkthroughs.body_html:
Sea walls: reflect waves (e.g. Scarborough). Expensive (~£6,000/m) and ugly but effective.

Groynes: trap sand from longshore drift — build wider beach that absorbs wave energy.

Rock armour (rip-rap): granite boulders absorb wave force.

Gabions: wire cages of rocks — cheap, short-lived.

Beach nourishment: pump sand from offshore onto eroding beach (Bournemouth).

Dune regeneration: plant marram grass to stabilise sand dunes.

Managed retreat: let the sea flood low-value farmland; build new salt marshes that absorb storm energy (Medmerry, Sussex).

Holderness (East Yorkshire) is one of Europe's fastest-eroding coastlines — averaging ~2 m per year.

Soft boulder clay cliffs undercut by powerful North Sea waves.

Settlements like Mappleton are protected with rock groynes; villages like Skipsea are not — homes literally fall into the sea each year.

mcqs.q: Which is an example of SOFT engineering?

options: Allowing low-value land to flood and relocating people
Removing all sand from a beach

numericals.q: Approximately how many METRES of coastline does Holderness lose each year on average?
numericals.hint: About 2 metres a year — fastest in Europe.

free_texts.q: What hard engineering feature is a wooden or rock fence built into the sea to trap sand? One word.
free_texts.hint: Often spelled with a 'y' in UK English.
